questions.q: What does SES with alpha = 1 equal?
why: Correct: l(t) = y(t), so the level is the last value.
The mean needs a very small alpha, not alpha = 1.
Drift has a slope. SES is flat.

questions.q: α = 0.4, old level 100, new value 110. What is the new level?
What is the weight of the value 3 steps back when alpha = 0.5?
A demand series climbs by about 2 units every week. You use SES. What is the typical error pattern?
options: The forecasts are always too low (the model lags)
The forecasts are always too high
The errors are random with mean zero
why: Correct: SES forecasts a flat level, so a rising series stays above the forecast.
The opposite would happen on a falling series.
A trend causes errors with the same sign. They are not random.

questions.q: Which data type fits SES best?
options: Noisy values around a stable or slowly moving level
Sales with a strong weekly pattern
A series with a yearly season and growth
why: Correct: SES has only a level.
A weekly pattern needs a seasonal method.

questions.q: You tune alpha on the full dataset and then test on the last 20% of it. What is wrong?
options: Alpha has seen the test data (leakage), so the test error is too optimistic
The test set is too small
why: Correct: tune on the training part only.
Tuning on all data leaks the future into the model.
Alpha is tuned all the time, on training data.
Size is not the issue. Leakage is.

questions.q: For the data 10, 14, 12, 16 and α = 0.5 with l(1) = 10, what is the forecast for step 10?
questions.why: The final level is 14 (see the lesson), and SES forecasts the same level for all future steps.
